title: Dictionaries
subtitle: Stat Sheets and Spell Books
martuIntro:
A list remembers order. It does not remember *meaning*. Which number is Lucky's armor? Which is his mana? A dictionary keeps a tag on every value. At the Institute, every student had a record like this. Mine said 'talks too little'.
You have seen dictionaries already: the spell book, the mana bars, and `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]` when you held the barrier. A lot of that code felt like a wall, yes? Tonight we read it one key at a time.
goals: Write a dictionary with keys in quotes, `:` and commas, and say why keys have quotes when box names don't
Read a value by its key, and mend a KeyError caused by spelling, capitals or a skipped level
Change a value and add a key, including `hero["mana"] = hero["mana"] - cost`
Ask whether a key is in a dictionary with `in` and `not in`
Use a key kept in a variable: `book[spell_name]`, not `book["spell_name"]`
Read and change values inside values: `hero["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]`
Read from a list of sheets, like `roster[2]["name"]`
Build a spell from variables and store it by name: `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`
Get a value, compare it, and act on it with `if` / `elif` / `else`, like holding the barrier

questions.explain: `roster[1]` is row 1, counting from 0: `["Gearshift", 20]`. Then `[1]` is item 1 of that row: 20. Outer number first, then inner.

The call hands over 9, so `affinity` is 9 inside the recipe. `total` is 18, and `return` hands 18 back to the `print`. If the recipe had no `return`, nothing would come back, and `print` would show `None`.

exercises.title: Which number is which?
exercises.martu:
A list remembers order. It does not remember *meaning*.
Here is Lucky as a [[list]]: his name, his magical affinity, his max mana and his armor bonus, in that order.
Print his armor bonus. Which position is it? Count from 0, yes?

anotherWay.label: Positions under the list
anotherWay.text:
Each item has a position, counting from 0:
```text
["Lucky", 13, 26, 3]
    0     1   2  3
```
Nothing in the list says which number is armor. Only the order does.

anotherWay.label: Lockers with no tags
anotherWay.text: A row of lockers with no tags. You must remember that locker 3 holds the armor. Forget once, and you grab the wrong thing.
My chalk wall is a good list: its order IS its meaning, oldest gap first. A hero's numbers have no order like that. They have meanings.
Count from 0: name 0, affinity 1, max mana 2, armor 3.

Write `print(lucky[3])` in place of `print(lucky[2])`.

exercises.title: Make a sheet
exercises.martu:
A [[dictionary]] keeps a tag on every value. Python calls the tag a [[key]]. Run the Example: Bomb Shell's sheet.
Curly brackets hold the sheet. Each line inside is a key, a colon, its value, then a comma.
Wait: quotes on a name? A box's name never has quotes: `mana = 26`. A key is text inside the sheet, so it does: `{"mana": 26}`. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. *Box* here means a variable, like `mana = 26`. A key is never a box.
Gearshift's sheet. Copy the keys exactly:
```text
GEARSHIFT
name               Gearshift
magical_affinity   10
max_mana           20
armor_bonus        3
```

anotherWay.label: Wait, quotes on names?
anotherWay.text:
A box's name (a variable) never has quotes: `mana = 26`. A key inside a dictionary is a piece of text, so it does: `{"mana": 26}`.
Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. *Box* here means a variable, like `mana = 26`. A key is never a box.

anotherWay.label: Keys and values in one big box
anotherWay.text:
The sheet is one big box. Inside, every value has its key:
```text
gearshift
+------------------------+
| "name"     "Gearshift" |
| "max_mana"          20 |
+------------------------+
```

anotherWay.label: A stat sheet
anotherWay.text: A stat sheet names every line: *armor bonus: 3*. You find a line by its name, not its number. A dictionary works the same way.

1. `gearshift = {` opens the sheet.
2. Each line: a key in quotes, `:`, the value, `,`.
3. `}` closes the sheet.
At the Institute, each student had a record card: a tag and a value on every line. Mine said *talks too little*. Python keeps the same kind of card.
In the spell book part, `spell = {...}` held three keys: `"mana_cost"`, `"required_affinity"` and `"spell_function"`. Each key had quotes, a colon and a value. That was a dictionary.

checkpoints.text: Make `gearshift` with the keys `"name"`, `"magical_affinity"`, `"max_mana"` and `"armor_bonus"`. Any value is fine for now, like 0.
hints: Each line inside the curly brackets is a key in quotes, a colon, a value, then a comma. Copy each key from the comment, letter for letter.
In the Example, `"dexterity": 6,` is one line: the key in quotes, `:`, the value, a comma.
Write one line for each key, like `"max_mana": 0,`, under `gearshift = {`.

campaignLink.why: You filled in a dictionary like this in the spell book part. Every key had quotes, a colon and a value. Now you know why the keys had quotes.

exercises.takeaway: A dictionary is `{ }` holding `"key": value` lines with commas. Keys are text, so they have quotes.

predict.explain: No quotes means look inside the box with this label. There is no box called `mana`, only a key inside `hero`, so Python stops: *not defined*. With quotes, `hero["mana"]` reads the key: 26.

exercises.title: Read by key
exercises.martu:
To read a value, write the sheet's name, then the key in square brackets: `gearshift["mana"]`. Python finds the key and hands you its value.
The brackets look like a list's. Inside, a list wants a position. A dictionary wants a key.
Then let the code build the line, the way you did in Unit 1.

anotherWay.label: Sheet, then key
anotherWay.text:
```text
gearshift["mana"]
    |        |
  sheet     key -> 20
```
First the sheet's name, then the key in square brackets.

1. `gearshift["name"]` gives `"Gearshift"`.
2. `+ ": "` glues on a colon and a space.
3. `str(gearshift["mana"])` gives `"20"`.
4. `+ " mana"` glues on the last word.
Reading a key is like finding *armor bonus* on a stat sheet and reading across. You look for the key, not the line number.
The sheet's name, then the key in square brackets: `gearshift["name"]`.

exercises.martu:
A [[KeyError]] means the sheet has no key spelled exactly like that. Capitals count. Spaces count. `"Max_Mana"` and `"max_mana"` are two different keys to Python.
Read the last line of the message. It names the key Python could not find. Then look at how the sheet spells it. Python shows keys in `'` marks, like `KeyError: 'Max_Mana'`. Same text.

anotherWay.label: How Python finds a key
anotherWay.text:
1. Python takes the key you wrote, letter by letter.
2. It looks for a key in the sheet spelled exactly the same.
3. None? It stops with `KeyError` and the key you wrote.

```text
before:  "mana": 20
after:   "mana": 14

```

Like a scoreboard: read the old score, work out the new one, and write it over the old one. The key stays; the number changes.

items.title: Why Does This Work? Keys and .get()
items.summary: Why a key can only appear once, how `.get()` avoids a KeyError, and why `in` is fast.
items.body:
Three things that make dictionaries work. Read them when you like. Nothing here is scored.
*Keys are unique.* A sheet has only one of each key. Give a key a value again, and the new value takes the old one's place:
```python
hero = {"name": "Moth", "glug": 1}
hero["glug"] = 3
print(hero)
```
It prints `{'name': 'Moth', 'glug': 3}`. There is still only one `"glug"`. When Python prints a whole sheet it uses `'` marks. Same text.
*A default instead of an error.* Reading a key that is not there stops the program with a [[KeyError]]. [[.get()|`.get()`]] asks more gently. `hero.get("glug", 0)` gives the value when the key is there, and 0 when it is not:
```python
hero = {"name": "Moth", "mana": 7}
print(hero.get("mana", 0))
print(hero.get("glug", 0))
```
It prints 7, then 0. No KeyError.
*Fast questions.* To find a value in a list, Python checks the items one by one, like opening a row of lockers. A dictionary works like the index at the back of a book: Python jumps straight to the key. So `"Glow" in spell_book` takes about the same time for 3 spells or 3,000.

exercises.title: Abilities inside
exercises.martu:
Some values are dictionaries too. Bomb Shell's `"abilities"` is a whole little sheet, kept inside the big one. Boxes in boxes, yes?
*Get it out of the dictionary: outer key, then inner key.* `bomb_shell["abilities"]` opens the inner card. Then `["wisdom"]` reads one line of it.

anotherWay.label: Boxes in boxes
anotherWay.text:
```text
bomb_shell
+---------------------------+
| "name" -> "Bomb Shell"    |
| "mana" -> 24              |
| "abilities" ->            |
|  +---------------------+  |
|  | "dexterity" -> 6    |  |
|  | "wisdom"    -> 8    |  |
|  | "magical_affinity"  |  |
|  |             -> 12   |  |
|  +---------------------+  |
+---------------------------+
```
The first key opens the big box's `"abilities"` drawer. The second key reads one line inside it.

anotherWay.label: Left to right
anotherWay.text:
1. `bomb_shell` is the whole sheet.
2. `bomb_shell["abilities"]` is the inner card: `{'dexterity': 6, 'wisdom': 8, ...}`.
3. `bomb_shell["abilities"]["wisdom"]` is one line of that card: 8.
Each pair of brackets goes one level in.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: Holding the barrier, the campaign read `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]`. The caster's sheet, then its abilities card, then one line. Same two keys in a row.
Institute records had a pocket on the back for the student's ability card. To read a score, you opened the record, then the pocket. Nobody found it on the front page.

exercises.title: Change inside
exercises.martu:
Reading inside is half the job. Writing inside uses the same path, on the left of `=`.
*Get it, change it, put it back.* The right side reads the old value, and Python works it out first. Then the left side puts the new value back in the same spot.
Get it into a variable, change it, then put it back with the same two keys on the left, as in the Example.

anotherWay.label: Get it, change it, put it back
anotherWay.text:
1. Get it: `dex = bomb_shell["abilities"]["dexterity"]` puts 6 in `dex`.
2. Change it: `dex + 2` is 8.
3. Put it back: `bomb_shell["abilities"]["dexterity"] = dex + 2` stores 8 in the same spot, inside `"abilities"`.
The wisdom next to it does not change.

anotherWay.label: Same path, both lines
anotherWay.text:
```text
get it:       6 -> dex
change it:    dex + 2 is 8
put it back:  8 -> ["abilities"]
                   ["dexterity"]
```
The first line and the last line walk the same two keys. One reads, one writes.
A score sheet in a binder: find the page, find the line, read the number, rub it out, write the new one in the same line. You don't start a new sheet.

anotherWay.text: Holding the barrier, the campaign wrote `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - spell["mana_cost"]`. Read the old value, change it, put it back. Here the spot is one level deeper.

anotherWay.label: In one line
anotherWay.text: The campaign did it in one line: `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - cost`. The same path on both sides. Both ways pass.

exercises.title: The roster
exercises.martu:
Four heroes, four sheets. A list holds them all, in order. The list remembers order. Each sheet remembers meaning.
To read one line, give the position first, then the key. `roster[2]` is the third sheet, since positions count from 0. `roster[2]["name"]` is its name.
A hero's name is not a position. `roster["Lucky"]` stops Python: a list only takes numbers in its brackets.

anotherWay.label: A row of sheets
anotherWay.text:
```text
roster
  [0]  oogrish
  [1]  gearshift
  [2]  bomb_shell
  [3]  lucky

roster[2]["name"]
  [2]      -> the bomb_shell sheet
  ["name"] -> "Bomb Shell"
```
The list is numbered. Each sheet inside it has its own keys.

1. `roster[0]`: the first sheet, Oogrish's.
2. `["abilities"]`: his ability card.
3. `["intelligence"]`: one line of the card, 17.
Numbers for the list, keys in quotes for the sheets.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: Every Module 2 part ended with `for member in party.members:`. That list was the roster: four sheets, in order. Each `member` was one whole sheet, read by key.
The Institute kept its records in a drawer, in order. To find one, you counted to the right folder. To read it, you used the keys inside.

exercises.title: A spell book of spells
exercises.martu:
A spell book is a dictionary of spells. Each key is a spell's name. Each value is a little sheet of its own: what the spell costs, and the affinity it needs.
To add a page, build the spell from your variables. Then store it under its name: `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`.
No quotes around `spell_name`. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. The box holds `"Lantern Ward"`, so that is the page you get.
Then ask first, as the campaign did: `if spell_name not in spell_book:`, with the store line indented under it. A page that is already there stays as it is.

anotherWay.label: A book of pages
anotherWay.text:
```text
spell_book
  "Glow"         -> {cost 2,
                     need 3}
  "Lantern Ward" -> {cost 6,
                     need 9}
```
`spell_name` holds the page's title. `spell` holds the page.

1. `spell_name` holds `"Lantern Ward"`.
2. `spell_book[spell_name]`: Python looks inside the box and finds `"Lantern Ward"`.
3. `= spell` stores the whole spell sheet on that page.
4. Glow's page is still there.
5. `if spell_name not in spell_book:` asks first, so a name that already has a page keeps it.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In `add_spell()`, you replaced each placeholder in the `spell` dictionary, then wrote `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`. That is this exercise. The campaign's names were the recipe's ingredients; here they are plain variables.
My spell book has a tab for each spell, with its name in ink. Behind each tab: the cost and what it needs. A new spell gets a new tab. The old tabs stay.

exercises.martu:
Holding the barrier was three moves: get it, compare, act.
*Get it:* read the value out of the sheet, through every key on the way. *Compare:* is it lower than what the spell needs? *Act:* print a warning, or cast.
The game hands you `caster`, as it did in the campaign:
```text
caster (from the game)
  "name"      -> "Bomb Shell"
  "mana"      -> 24
  "abilities" ->
    "magical_affinity" -> 12
```
One rule from the campaign: exactly enough still casts.

anotherWay.label: Get it, compare, act
anotherWay.text:
1. Get it: `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]` is 12. `spell["required_affinity"]` is 9.
2. Compare: is 12 lower than 9? No. Skip that branch.
3. Get it: `caster["mana"]` is 24. `spell["mana_cost"]` is 6. Is 24 lower than 6? No.
4. Act: the `else`. 24 - 6 is 18. Print 18.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: The `hold-the-barrier` comments said: if the affinity is lower than the spell's required affinity, say they aren't skilled enough. Otherwise, if the mana is lower than the cost, say so. Otherwise, cast and subtract. This is that chain, with `print` for `print_prompt`.

anotherWay.label: Three doors
anotherWay.text:
```text
affinity too low? -yes-> Not skilled
      | no
mana too low? ---yes---> Needs mana
      | no
else: spend, print the mana
```
Python takes the first door that opens, and only that one.

items.title: Dictionaries Quiz
items.summary: Eight questions on keys, sheets inside sheets, rosters and spell books. Retake as often as you like.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only, letter for letter. The key is `"Glow"` with a capital G, so `"glow"` is not a key: `False`. 2 is a value, not a key, so `2 in pack` is `False` too.

questions.q: `spell_name` holds `"Glow"`. Which line prints Glow's cost?

whyWrong.0: With quotes, Python looks for a key spelled s-p-e-l-l-_-n-a-m-e. The book has no such key, so it stops with a KeyError.
whyWrong.2: Dictionaries are read with square brackets, not a dot. Python stops: `'dict' object has no attribute 'spell_name'`.

questions.explain: No quotes means look inside the box: `spell_name` holds `"Glow"`, so `spell_book[spell_name]` reads Glow's page, 2.

questions.q: Put the lines in order (with their indents). Build the spell from `cost` and `needed`, then store it under `spell_name`.
questions.explain: Make the variables first, then the spell that uses them, then store it. `spell_book[spell_name]` has no quotes, so the page is called Frost Veil. With quotes it would be called spell_name.
Outer key, then inner key. `hero["abilities"]` is Lucky's inner card. `["strength"]` reads one line of it: 17. One key alone would print the whole card.

questions.q: Fill the blank so the hero pays `cost` from their mana. The program should print 18.
questions.explain: The right side reads the old mana, 24, and takes away `cost`. The left side stores 18 back in the same key. This is the campaign's mana line.

questions.q: This program stops with `KeyError: 'wisdom'`. Mend it so it prints Lucky's wisdom.
questions.explain: Wisdom is not on the big sheet. It lives inside `"abilities"`, so the read needs the outer key first: `hero["abilities"]["wisdom"]`.
`roster[1]` is the second sheet, Lucky's, because positions count from 0. Then `["mana"]` reads his mana: 26.
During the call, `book` holds the spell book and `name` holds `"Glow"`. `book[name]` looks inside `name`, so it reads Glow's page and hands back 2.

items.intro:
Mar'tu copies each hero's record into the cabin ledger, Institute-style: the same keys on every sheet.
Three parts, in order: A. the sheets, B. let the code combine it, C. the roster.

```text
hero        INT WIS DEX STR AFF
Oogrish      17  17  14  13   9
Gearshift    14  15  13  17  10
Bomb Shell   14   8   6  15  12
Lucky        13  12  15  17  13
```

Lucky has a list, of course.

items.title: The Barrier, From Blank
items.summary: Write the whole `cast_spell` recipe from a blank page, the way the campaign's barrier worked.
items.martu:
The barrier, from a blank page. You have every piece now: `not in`, two keys in a row, `if` / `elif` / `else`, and a change by key. Write `cast_spell(caster, spell_name)`:
1. If the name is not in the caster's `"spell_book"`, print a message.
2. Otherwise, read the spell from the book.
3. If the affinity is lower than the spell's `"required_affinity"`, say they are not skilled enough.
4. Else, if the mana is lower than its `"mana_cost"`, say it needs more mana.
5. Else, subtract the cost from `caster["mana"]`.
Your recipe changes the sheet it is handed, as the campaign's did. My check calls it with other casters and other spells, only inside the check.

anotherWay.label: The campaign's order
anotherWay.text:
1. Ask the book: `not in` first.
2. Read the spell: the book, by the name.
3. Compare the affinity: `<`.
4. `elif`: compare the mana.
5. `else`: take the cost from the mana, by key.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `hold-the-barrier` handed you this recipe with its `not in` question already written, and you filled in the chain. The campaign stopped after the message with `return`; an `else` does the same job here. Can they cast? was the chain on its own.

anotherWay.label: Doors in doors
anotherWay.text:
```text
name not in book? --> message
  else: read the spell
    affinity low? --> not skilled
    mana low? -----> more mana
    else: spend the cost
```
Python takes the first door that opens, and only that one.

items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 5. To pass the Quick Check, get 2 of the 3 right.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only. `"Spark"` is a key: `True`. `"Glow"` is not a key, so `not in` gives `True`. 4 is a value, not a key, so `4 in book` is `False`.

whyWrong.0: `name` with no quotes is a box name, so Python looks for a box called `name` and stops: NameError. Keys are text, so they need quotes.
whyWrong.1: `=` puts a value in a box. Inside a sheet, a colon goes between each key and its value.
whyWrong.3: A comma is missing after `"Pell"`, so Python stops: invalid syntax.

questions.explain: Keys are text, so each one has quotes. A colon goes between a key and its value, and a comma between the pairs. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.
No quotes means look inside the box: `spell_name` holds `"Spark"`, so Python reads Spark's page, 5. `book["spell_name"]`, with quotes, would stop with a KeyError.

items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 5. To pass the Quick Check, get 2 of the 3 right.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only. `"Iron Bark"` is a key: `True`. `"Stone Skin"` is a key too, so `not in` gives `False`. 6 is a value, not a key, so `6 in wards` is `False`.

whyWrong.1: `name` with no quotes is a box name, so Python looks for a box called `name` and stops: NameError. Keys are text, so they need quotes.
whyWrong.2: `=` puts a value in a box. Inside a sheet, a colon goes between each key and its value.
whyWrong.3: A colon is missing after `"name"`, so Python stops: invalid syntax.

questions.explain: Keys are text, so each one has quotes. A colon goes between a key and its value, and a comma between the pairs. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.
No quotes means look inside the box: `ward_name` holds `"Stone Skin"`, so Python reads Stone Skin's page, 4. `wards["ward_name"]`, with quotes, would stop with a KeyError.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Dictionaries
items.summary: Everything from Unit 5 on one page. Printable.

entries.note: Curly brackets hold the sheet (a dictionary). Each line is a key in quotes, a colon, its value and a comma. (Lesson: Stat Sheets)

entries.concept: Box names have no quotes. Keys do.
entries.note: A box's name (a variable) never has quotes. A key is text inside the sheet, so it does. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.
Square brackets, with the key in quotes, read one value.
The right side reads the old mana and takes 3 away. The left side stores the answer under the same key. You've seen this: `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - spell["mana_cost"]`.
A key the sheet doesn't have yet is added. A key it has is changed: a key is never there twice.
2 is a value, not a key, so `2 in book` is `False`. You've seen this: `if spell_name not in caster["spell_book"]:`.
No quotes: Python looks inside `spell_name` and finds `"Warm Hands"`. `book["spell_name"]`, with quotes, looks for a key spelled s-p-e-l-l-_-n-a-m-e, and stops with a KeyError.
Outer key, then inner key. One key alone gives the whole inner card. You've seen this: `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]`. (Lesson: Sheets Inside Sheets)

entries.concept: Change a value inside a card
entries.note: Get it, change it, put it back. `w` gets the old wisdom, 8. The next line puts the new one, 11, back in the same spot, with the same two keys on the left of `=`.
Position first, counting from 0, then the key. A list remembers order; each sheet remembers meaning. In the campaign, a list like this was `party.members`.
The key comes from the variable `name`, so the page is called Warm Hands. You've seen this: `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`.

entries.concept: Store only when it is new
entries.note: `not in` asks first, so a page that is already there stays as it is. The store line is indented under the `if`, so it runs only when the name is new.
Get it: read the value through every key. Compare: `<` asks *lower than*, so exactly enough still casts. Act: only one branch of the chain runs. You've seen this: holding the barrier.
`.get` gives the second value when the key is missing, in place of a KeyError. (Article: Why Does This Work? Keys and .get())

entries.concept: Error: a key with no quotes
entries.note: NameError: name 'name' is not defined. With no quotes, `name` is a box name. Keys are text: `"name"`.
SyntaxError: cannot assign to literal here. Maybe you meant '==' instead of '='? Python's guess is wrong here: inside a sheet, a colon goes between a key and its value.
SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma? After a number, Python names that line. After text, it names the next line.
SyntaxError: ':' expected after dictionary key. Every key needs a colon before its value.
KeyError: 'Mana'. No key is spelled exactly like that. Check the spelling, the capitals and the spaces.
KeyError: 'wisdom'. Wisdom lives inside `"abilities"`. Read the outer key first.
AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'mana'. Read a sheet with square brackets and the key in quotes.
TypeError: 'dict' object is not callable. Round brackets call a recipe. A sheet takes square brackets.

entries.concept: Error: a position on a sheet
entries.note: KeyError: 0. A sheet has no positions, only keys.

entries.concept: Error: a name as a list position
entries.note: TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str. A list takes a position number.

entries.concept: Error: a variable's name in quotes
entries.note: KeyError: 'spell_name'. With quotes, Python looks for those exact letters. Without them, it looks inside the variable.
